First, he was like a lamp: for as a lamp is not light by its essence and does not shine of itself, but by the flame set in it, so John was not light by essence[[John 1:8||]], nor did he shine of himself, but by sharing in the divine light, that is, by the grace of Christ poured into him, which shone through John's body in word and deed, as the flame of a lamp shines through its horn panes. And as a lamp with its flame is dimmed when the light of day comes on, so when Christ shone forth in words and miracles John began to be dimmed, as he himself foretold: [[John 3:30|He must increase: but I must decrease|Illum oportet crescere, me autem minui]]. John was also a lamp burning with the fire of divine love, by which he rejoiced at Christ's excellence, as he says: [[John 3:29|the friend of the bridegroom, who standeth and heareth Him, rejoiceth with joy because of the bridegroom's voice|Amicus sponsi qui stat et audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi]]. John burned also with the zeal of justice, with which he rebuked Herod[[Matt 14:4||]], and with the flame of love for his neighbours. And he had words vehemently on fire, saying: [[Luke 3:7|Ye offspring of vipers, who hath shewed you to flee from the wrath to come?|Genimina viperarum, quis ostendit vobis fugere a ventura ira?]] [[Luke 3:8|Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of penance|facite ergo dignos fructus pœnitentiæ]]. He was, besides, shining with the rays of wisdom, and splendid in a most excellent life that was an example to others, and in his preaching.

paras.t: Sic et quilibet niti debet ad hoc, ut sit lucerna ardens et lucens, quatenus et lumen gratiæ aptum in eo locum inveniat, et ipse in se ipso divina caritate fervescat, atque in contemplatione sapientiæ fulgeat, proximos quoque ad Dei amorem et veritatis notitiam conetur inducere: sicque gratia animæ suæ redundet, manifestetur ac emicet in vultus gravitate, in morum probitate, in totius corporis gressu, omnique actu. Beati qui tales sunt: a quibus plus disto quam oriens ab occasu.
paras.en: So too every one ought to strive to be [[5:35|a burning and a shining light|lucerna ardens et lucens]]: so that the light of grace may find a fit place in him, and he may glow within himself with divine charity and shine in the contemplation of wisdom, and may try to lead his neighbours to the love of God and the knowledge of the truth; and so the grace of his soul may overflow, show itself and shine out in the gravity of his face, the uprightness of his ways, the gait of his whole body and his every act. Blessed are they who are such: from whom I am further off than the east is from the west.

paras.t: Vos autem voluistis exsultare spiritualiter ad horam, id est ad tempus modicum, in luce ejus, id est in perfectione, et gratia, et sanctitate, et doctrina Joannis, gaudendo de hoc quod habuistis tam sapientem Prophetam. Sed non diu duravit exsultatio illa, quia quum cœpit increpare vitia vestra, dixistis, Dæmonium habet; noluistisque credere verbis ejus quibus mihi testimonium reddidit. Et ut multi affirmant, Herodes etiam ad suggestionem Judæorum, clausit ac decollavit Joannem. Vel ideo dicit Salvator, quod Judæi voluerunt ad horam exsultare in luce Joannis, quia parati fuerunt eum pro Christo recipere, et in principio multi eorum obedierunt Joanni.
paras.en: [[5:35|and you were willing for a time to rejoice|Vos autem voluistis exsultare spiritualiter ad horam]] spiritually, for a short while, [[5:35|in his light|in luce ejus]], that is, in the perfection, grace, holiness and teaching of John, rejoicing that you had so wise a Prophet. But that rejoicing did not last long, because when he began to rebuke your vices you said, [[Matt 11:18|He hath a devil|Dæmonium habet]], and would not believe the words with which he bore witness to Me. And, as many affirm, Herod too, at the prompting of the Jews, shut up John and beheaded him[[Matt 14:3||]][[Matt 14:10||]]. Or the Saviour says that the Jews were willing for a time to rejoice in John's light because they were ready to receive him as the Christ, and at the beginning many of them obeyed John.

paras.t: Ego autem habeo testimonium majus Joanne, id est dignius testificatione Joannis facta de me. Et quod sit testimonium istud majus subjungitur. Opera enim quæ dedit mihi Pater ut perficiam ea, id est miraculosi effectus totam potestatem naturæ excedentes, quos Pater facit per me, et vult eos perfici, id est perfecte et excellentissimo modo fieri, a me; Ipsa opera quæ ego facio propria virtute, secundum quod Deus, et in quantum homo facio ea virtute Patris, imo totius Trinitatis, cujus est una potestas, testimonium perhibent de me, quia, id est quod, Pater me misit, videlicet, quod a Deo veni, et recta ago et prædico. Sicut enim veritas naturalis scientiæ probatur per rationis discursum, ex principiis per se notis, sic supernaturalis veritas fidei demonstratur per opera soli Deo possibilia, qui quum sit veritas, nunquam facit opera talia ad confirmationem erroris. Quoniam ergo talia multa fecit Jesus, certum est quod a Deo missus sit, verusque doctor consistat.
paras.en: [[5:36|But I have a greater testimony than that of John|Ego autem habeo testimonium majus Joanne]], that is, worthier than the testimony John gave of Me. And what this greater testimony is, is added: [[5:36|for the works which the Father hath given me to perfect|Opera enim quæ dedit mihi Pater ut perficiam ea]], that is, miraculous effects exceeding the whole power of nature, which the Father does through Me and wills to be perfected, that is, done perfectly and in the most excellent way, by Me: [[5:36|the works themselves which I do|Ipsa opera quæ ego facio]] by My own power as God, and as man by the power of the Father, nay of the whole Trinity, whose power is one, [[5:36|give testimony of me, that the Father hath sent me|testimonium perhibent de me, quia, id est quod, Pater me misit]], namely that I have come from God, and do and preach what is right. For as the truth of natural science is proved by the reasoning of the mind from principles known of themselves, so the supernatural truth of faith is shown by works possible to God alone, who, since He is the truth, never does such works to confirm error. Since, then, Jesus did many such works, it is certain that He was sent by God and is a true teacher.

paras.t: Et qui misit me Pater. Duplex est missio Filii Dei: Una invisibilis, qua Pater a principio mundi misit æternam Sapientiam ad mentes electorum, per hoc quod illuminavit eas gratia suæ Sapientiæ increatæ ac genitæ. Quum enim in Patre sit auctoritas quoad Filium, atque in Filio subauctoritas quantum ad Patrem, convenit Patrem mittere Filium, etiam secundum divinam naturam. Simili ratione Pater et Filius mittunt Spiritum Sanctum, quia in ipsis est auctoritas quoad Spiritum Sanctum, et in Spiritu Sancto subauctoritas ad Patrem et Filium, quasi ad unum principium unumque spiratorem ac fontem. De hac nempe spirituali et invisibili missione Verbi, habetur in libro Sapientiæ: Mitte illam de cælis sanctis tuis et a sede magnitudinis tuæ, ut mecum sit et mecum laboret. Alia est missio Filii Dei temporalis atque visibilis, quæ dicitur incarnatio ejus. Nec dubium quin Christus in mundo conversans, mittebatur a Patre ad omnia loca et opera quæcumque accessit aut fecit. Imo Christus secundum quod Deus, misit se ipsum secundum quod homo.
paras.en: [[5:37|And the Father himself who hath sent me|Et qui misit me Pater]]. The sending of the Son of God is twofold. One is invisible, by which the Father from the beginning of the world sent the eternal Wisdom into the minds of the elect, by enlightening them with the grace of His uncreated and begotten Wisdom. For since in the Father there is authority with respect to the Son, and in the Son a being-from-authority with respect to the Father, it belongs to the Father to send the Son, even according to the divine nature. For a like reason the Father and the Son send the Holy Ghost, because in them there is authority with respect to the Holy Ghost, and in the Holy Ghost a being-from-authority with respect to the Father and the Son, as to one principle, one breather-forth and fountain. Of this spiritual and invisible sending of the Word we have in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 9:10|Send her out of thy holy heaven, and from the throne of thy majesty, that she may be with me, and may labour with me|Mitte illam de cælis sanctis tuis et a sede magnitudinis tuæ, ut mecum sit et mecum laboret]]. The other is the temporal and visible sending of the Son of God, which is called His incarnation[[Gal 4:4||]]. And there is no doubt that Christ, living in the world, was sent by the Father to every place He went to and every work He did. Indeed Christ as God sent Himself as man.

paras.t: Ipse testimonium perhibuit de me. Hoc specialiter accipi potest de testimonio Patris quo in baptismo locutus est: Hic est Filius meus dilectus. Nihilo minus a principio mundi perhibuit Pater testimonium Christo per oracula Patriarcharum, per vaticinia Prophetarum, per diversa sacramenta et gesta figuralia. Unde, secundum Augustinum, Nulla ætas vacavit a prophetia de Christo. Propter quod apud Lucam Zacharias disseruit: Erexit cornu salutis nobis, sicut locutus est per os sanctorum qui a sæculo sunt Prophetarum ejus. Videtur autem Christus ad litteram loqui de testimonio vocis paternæ prætactæ. Loquitur enim nunc distinctim de triplici testimonio sibi perhibito, utpote Joannis, et operum, ac Patris.
paras.en: [[5:37|hath given testimony of me|Ipse testimonium perhibuit de me]]. This can be taken especially of the testimony of the Father, by which He spoke at the baptism: [[Matt 3:17|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]]. Yet from the beginning of the world the Father bore testimony to Christ through the oracles of the Patriarchs, the prophecies of the Prophets, and divers sacraments and figurative deeds. Hence, according to Augustine, no age was without prophecy of Christ. For which reason Zachary declared in Luke: [[Luke 1:69|And hath raised up an horn of salvation to us|Erexit cornu salutis nobis]], [[Luke 1:70|As he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who are from the beginning|sicut locutus est per os sanctorum qui a sæculo sunt Prophetarum ejus]]. But Christ seems in the letter to be speaking of the testimony of the Father's voice just touched on. For He is now speaking distinctly of the threefold testimony borne to Him, namely that of John, that of the works, and that of the Father.

paras.t: Neque vocem ejus unquam audistis. Quæritur, quomodo Salvator dicat Judæos nunquam audisse vocem Patris. Supra enim, capitulo tertio, dixit ad Nicodemum, Spiritus ubi vult spirat, et vocem ejus audis: quod melius intelligitur de Spiritu Sancto quam de vento. Sicut ergo Judæi audierunt vocem Spiritus Sancti, sic et Patris. Denique Joannes ait, Ego vox clamantis in deserto: ergo audiendo Joannem, audierunt vocem Patris. Sed et Christus est verbum et sermo Patris: de quo ad Hebræos dicit Apostolus, Vivus est sermo Dei, et efficax, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti. Quod enim id de increato Dei Verbo dicatur, elucescit ex eo quod subditur: Et non est ulla creatura invisibilis in conspectu ejus; omnia autem nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus ad quem nobis sermo. Itaque audiendo Christum, audierunt verbum sermonemque Patris, et per consequens vocem ipsius. Præterea, sacra Scriptura nonne vox Dei est, dicente Apostolo, Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata? Judæi ergo audiendo eloquia Prophetarum ac Moysis, audierunt vocem Dei. Moyses quoque ait in Deuteronomio: Probavimus hodie quod loquente Deo cum homine, vixerit homo; vocem ejus audivimus de medio ignis.
paras.en: [[5:37|neither have you heard his voice at any time|Neque vocem ejus unquam audistis]]. It is asked how the Saviour says that the Jews never heard the Father's voice. For above, in the third chapter, He said to Nicodemus: [[John 3:8|The Spirit breatheth where he will and thou hearest his voice|Spiritus ubi vult spirat, et vocem ejus audis]], which is better understood of the Holy Ghost than of the wind. As, then, the Jews heard the voice of the Holy Ghost, so too that of the Father. Again, John says, [[John 1:23|I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness|Ego vox clamantis in deserto]]: so in hearing John they heard the voice of the Father. Christ too is the Word and speech of the Father, of whom the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 4:12|the word of God is living and effectual and more piercing than any two edged sword|Vivus est sermo Dei, et efficax, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti]]. That this is said of the uncreated Word of God shines out from what is added: [[Heb 4:13|Neither is there any creature invisible in his sight: but all things are naked and open to his eyes, to whom our speech is|Et non est ulla creatura invisibilis in conspectu ejus; omnia autem nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus ad quem nobis sermo]]. So in hearing Christ they heard the Word and speech of the Father, and consequently His voice. Moreover, is not holy Scripture the voice of God, as the Apostle says, [[2 Tim 3:16|All scripture, inspired of God|Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata]]? So the Jews, in hearing the words of the Prophets and of Moses, heard the voice of God. Moses too says in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 5:24|have proved this day that God speaking with man, man hath lived|Probavimus hodie quod loquente Deo cum homine, vixerit homo]]; [[Deut 5:24|we have heard his voice out of the midst of the fire|vocem ejus audivimus de medio ignis]].

paras.t: Quidam expositores faciliter transeuntes dicunt, quod ideo Christus dixit istis perversis incredulisque Judæis, quod nunquam audierunt vocem Patris, quia non audierunt præinductum testimonium vocis paternæ de Filio in baptismo: Hic est Filius meus dilectus. Alii dicunt, quod ideo Christus ait, Neque vocem ejus unquam audistis, neque speciem ejus vidistis, ut insinuet Deum Patrem esse omnino incorporalem ac insensibilem, ita quod neque audiri potest neque videri sensu corporeo, quum non habeat os, linguam, et cetera instrumenta loquendi. Et quamvis per subjectam creaturam loquatur, tamen non auditur vox ejus, quasi ipse sit immediatus propriusque formator hujuscemodi vocis. — Sed quia Salvator duris et perfidis loquebatur Judæis, qui verba divina tradita in Scripturis non vere et spiritualiter intellexerunt, videtur sic exponendum: Neque vocem ejus, id est Scripturas sacras mihi testimonium perhibentes, a Patre revelatas, unquam audistis auribus cordis; sed grosse atque carnaliter, id est secundum litteram, quæ occidit, intellexistis eas. Juxta hunc modum Moyses locutus est Judæis in Deuteronomio: Vos vidistis universa magnalia Dei, et non dedit vobis Dominus cor intelligens et aures quæ possint audire, usque in præsentem diem. Huic expositioni sequentia quoque consonant, ut patebit.
paras.en: Some expositors, passing over it lightly, say that Christ told these perverse and unbelieving Jews that they had never heard the Father's voice because they had not heard the testimony of the Father's voice about the Son at the baptism, mentioned above: [[Matt 3:17|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]]. Others say that Christ says, *neither have you heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape*, to hint that God the Father is wholly incorporeal and beyond the senses, so that He can be neither heard nor seen by bodily sense, since He has no mouth, tongue or other instruments of speech. And though He speaks through a creature subject to Him, yet His voice is not heard as though He Himself were the immediate and proper former of that voice. — But since the Saviour was speaking to hard and faithless Jews, who did not understand truly and spiritually the divine words handed down in the Scriptures, it seems it should be expounded thus: *Neither have you heard his voice*, that is, the holy Scriptures revealed by the Father that bear witness to Me, *at any time* with the ears of the heart; but you have understood them grossly and carnally, that is, according to the letter, which killeth[[2 Cor 3:6||]]. In this way Moses spoke to the Jews in Deuteronomy: You have seen all the great works of God[[Deut 29:2||]], [[Deut 29:4|And the Lord hath not given you a heart to understand, and eyes to see, and ears that may hear, unto this present day|et non dedit vobis Dominus cor intelligens et aures quæ possint audire, usque in præsentem diem]]. What follows also agrees with this exposition, as will be plain.

paras.t: Neque speciem ejus vidistis. Hoc uno modo intelligi potest, quod non viderunt Deum per speciem, id est divinam essentiam, quomodo vident eum Beati in patria. Secundo, quod nec fide sincera puraque mente contemplati sunt Deum. Qui enim ait se nosse Deum, et mandata ejus non custodit, mendax est. — Quomodo ergo patres et vates veteris Testamenti speciem Dei vidisse scribuntur? dicente patriarcha Jacob: Vidi Dominum facie ad faciem. Et Isaias: Vidi (inquit) Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum. Daniel etiam perhibet se vidisse Antiquum dierum, et cujus capilli erant sicut lana alba. Et respondendum, quod non viderunt Deum in specie propria, sed aliena, in imaginatione formata, vel ab angelo in persona Dei apparente assumpta, vel alio modo consimili.
paras.en: [[5:37|nor seen his shape|Neque speciem ejus vidistis]]. This can be understood, in one way, that they did not see God by sight [*per speciem*], that is, the divine essence, as the Blessed see Him in the fatherland. Secondly, that they did not contemplate God even with sincere faith and a pure mind. For [[1 John 2:4|He who saith that he knoweth him and keepeth not his commandments is a liar|Qui enim ait se nosse Deum, et mandata ejus non custodit, mendax est]]. — How then are the fathers and prophets of the Old Testament written to have seen the shape of God? For the patriarch Jacob says: [[Gen 32:30|I have seen God face to face|Vidi Dominum facie ad faciem]]. And Isaias: [[Is 6:1|I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and elevated|Vidi (inquit) Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum]]. Daniel too testifies that he saw [[Dan 7:9|the ancient of days|Antiquum dierum]], whose hair was [[Dan 7:9|like clean wool|sicut lana alba]]. The answer is that they did not see God in His own shape, but in another's: one formed in the imagination, or taken by an angel appearing in the person of God, or in some other like way.

paras.t: Et verbum ejus, scilicet Dei Patris, non habetis in vobis manens. Quod primo accipi potest de unico Filio Patris, de quo dictum est: In principio erat Verbum. Hoc isti increduli non habuerunt manens, id est fixum ac habitans, in cordibus suis per fidem et caritatem. Unde Apostolus asserit Christum habitare per fidem in cordibus nostris. Propter quod dictum fuit superius: Et sui eum non receperunt. Secundo exponitur sic: Et verbum ejus non habetis in vobis manens, hoc est, divinis sermonibus et Scripturis non obeditis, sed vacui estis a cognitione formata et salutari memoria divinorum verborum. Quocontra ait Psalmista: In corde meo abscondi eloquia tua, ut non peccem tibi. Quemadmodum enim impii, quamvis subtiles, dicuntur non cognoscere Deum, quoniam non honorant eum ut Deum, sed factis negant; sic perversi et perfidi, quamvis in Scripturis promptissimi, dicuntur tamen non habere in se verbum Dei, quoniam eo abutuntur. Tertio sic: Et verbum ejus non habetis in vobis manens, id est, internam Dei inspirationem non percipitis, neque per revelationem occultam Filium Dei cognoscitis. Omnibus enim expositionibus istis concordant sequentia: quia quem misit ille, id est mihi Filio Dei misso a Patre cælesti, huic vos non creditis.
paras.en: [[5:38|And you have not his word abiding in you|Et verbum ejus non habetis in vobis manens]], the word of God the Father. This can be taken, first, of the only Son of the Father, of whom it is said: [[John 1:1|In the beginning was the Word|In principio erat Verbum]]. Him these unbelievers did not have *abiding*, that is, fixed and dwelling, in their hearts by faith and charity. Hence the Apostle asserts that [[Eph 3:17|Christ may dwell by faith in your hearts|Christum habitare per fidem in cordibus nostris]] [Denis: “in our hearts”]. For which reason it was said above: [[John 1:11|and his own received him not|Et sui eum non receperunt]]. Secondly it is expounded thus: *you have not his word abiding in you*, that is, you do not obey the divine words and Scriptures, but are empty of the formed knowledge and saving remembrance of the divine words. Against this the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:11|Thy words have I hidden in my heart, that I may not sin against thee|In corde meo abscondi eloquia tua, ut non peccem tibi]]. For as the wicked, however subtle, are said not to know God because they do not honour Him as God, but in their works deny Him[[Tit 1:16||]], so the perverse and faithless, however ready they are in the Scriptures, are yet said not to have the word of God in them, because they abuse it. Thirdly thus: *you have not his word abiding in you*, that is, you do not perceive God's inward inspiration, nor know the Son of God by hidden revelation. For with all these expositions what follows agrees: [[5:38|for whom he hath sent|quia quem misit ille]], that is, Me, the Son of God sent by the heavenly Father, [[5:38|him you believe not|huic vos non creditis]].

paras.t: Et quia Salvator jam tetigit quod vocem Patris, id est Scripturas de Christo loquentes, non recte ac spiritualiter intellexerunt, sed superficialiter ac ruditer nimis, idcirco subjungit ac hortatur: Scrutamini, id est, solerter discutite, investigate, advertite, Scripturas legis ac Prophetarum. Est ergo quædam scrutatio divinorum bona, discreta ac salutaris, non ex curiositate, præsumptione vel infidelitate quadam procedens, sed ex aviditate agnoscendæ veritatis propter Dei amorem atque honorem. De qua in Actibus Apostolorum Lucas testatur, de Thessalonicensibus loquens: Nobiliores ex eis susceperunt verbum Dei cum omni aviditate, quotidie scrutantes Scripturas, si hæc se ita haberent; et Psalmista, Mirabilia testimonia tua, ideo scrutata est ea anima mea. Alia est scrutatio curiosa et immoderata, qua quis difficilia ultra propriam capacitatem nititur discutere, incomprehensibilia capere, Scripturas sacras proprio ingenio mensurare ac judicare. De qua Salomon fassus est: Scrutator majestatis opprimetur a gloria; et in Ecclesiastico, Fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris.
paras.en: And since the Saviour has already touched on their not understanding the Father's voice, that is, the Scriptures that speak of Christ, rightly and spiritually, but superficially and too crudely, He adds this exhortation: [[5:39|Search the scriptures|Scrutamini Scripturas]], that is, examine, investigate and attend carefully to the Scriptures of the law and the Prophets. There is, then, a good, discreet and saving searching of divine things, which proceeds not from curiosity, presumption or some unbelief, but from eagerness to know the truth, for the love and honour of God. Of this Luke testifies in the Acts of the Apostles, speaking of the Thessalonians: [[Acts 17:11|Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, who received the word with all eagerness, daily searching the scriptures, whether these things were so|Nobiliores ex eis susceperunt verbum Dei cum omni aviditate, quotidie scrutantes Scripturas, si hæc se ita haberent]] [Denis's text applies the praise to those of Thessalonica]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 118:129|Thy testimonies are wonderful: therefore my soul hath sought them|Mirabilia testimonia tua, ideo scrutata est ea anima mea]]. The other is a curious and immoderate searching, by which someone tries to discuss difficult things beyond his own capacity, to grasp incomprehensible things, and to measure and judge the holy Scriptures by his own wit. Of this Solomon said: [[Prov 25:27|he that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory|Scrutator majestatis opprimetur a gloria]]; and in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 3:22|search not into things above thy ability|Fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris]].

paras.t: Quia vos putatis in ipsis, id est in notitia Scripturarum, vitam æternam habere, id est æternam beatitudinem promereri ac adipisci: quod et ita fuisset, si eas vere et efficaciter intellexissetis. Sed quia oppositum contigit propter Judæorum duritiam, aptissime dixit Christus, Quia putatis, id est, inaniter æstimatis: defraudati namque estis spe vestra.
paras.en: [[5:39|for you think in them to have life everlasting|quia vos putatis in ipsis vitam æternam habere]]: in them, that is, in the knowledge of the Scriptures; *to have life everlasting*, that is, to merit and gain eternal beatitude. And so it would have been, if you had understood them truly and to good effect. But since the opposite happened because of the hardness of the Jews, Christ said most fittingly, *you think*, that is, you vainly suppose: for you have been cheated of your hope.

paras.t: Et illæ Scripturæ sunt quæ testimonium perhibent de me. In libris etenim Moysis et Prophetarum, non solum prænuntiatur Christi adventus et incarnatio Verbi, sed etiam determinatur tempus adventus, locus nativitatis, modus conversationis et qualitas passionis: sed et resurrectio et ascensio Christi illic prænuntiatur. De ejus enim adventu, cecinit Isaias: Puer natus est nobis, et filius datus est nobis. De tempore vero adventus Christi, locutus est Jacob in Genesi: Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda, donec veniat qui mittendus est: et Daniel, Septuaginta hebdomades (videlicet hebdomades annorum lunarium) abbreviatæ sunt super populum tuum, ut deleatur iniquitas, et impleatur visio et prophetia, et ungatur Sanctus Sanctorum. Modus quoque adventus istius, videlicet quod Christus venit et conversatus est cum hominibus in maxima paupertate et humilitate, descriptus fuit per Jeremiam: Quare quasi colonus venturus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum? Et per Zachariam: Ecce Rex tuus veniet tibi mansuetus; ipse pauper. Itemque Psalmista: Pauper sum ego, et in laboribus a juventute mea. Præterea, de loco nativitatis, per Michæam: Et tu, Bethlehem Ephrata, ex te mihi egredietur qui sit dominator in Israel. Modum quoque conceptionis Isaias deprompsit: Ecce virgo concipiet et pariet filium; rursusque, Ascendet, inquit, quasi virgultum coram eo, et quasi radix de terra sitienti. Hoc est quod prophetavit Psalmista: Descendet sicut pluvia in vellus, et sicut stillicidia stillantia super terram. De passione vero et tempore passionis, Daniel dixit: Post hebdomades sexaginta duas occidetur Christus; et Isaias, Ipse vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra, et sicut ovis ad occisionem ducetur. Et summatim stringendo, vix aliquid in Evangelio continetur, quod non in veteri Testamento inveniatur prædictum. Propter quod ait Apostolus, se segregatum in Evangelium, quod ante promiserat Deus per Prophetas suos in Scripturis sanctis de Filio suo.
paras.en: [[5:39|And the same are they that give testimony of me|Et illæ Scripturæ sunt quæ testimonium perhibent de me]]. For in the books of Moses and the Prophets not only are the coming of Christ and the incarnation of the Word foretold, but the time of His coming, the place of His birth, the manner of His life and the kind of His passion are fixed; and the resurrection and ascension of Christ are foretold there too. Of His coming Isaias sang: [[Is 9:6|a CHILD IS BORN to us, and a son is given to us|Puer natus est nobis, et filius datus est nobis]]. Of the time of Christ's coming Jacob spoke in Genesis: [[Gen 49:10|The sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda|Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda]], [[Gen 49:10|till he come that is to be sent|donec veniat qui mittendus est]]; and Daniel: [[Dan 9:24|Seventy weeks are shortened upon thy people|Septuaginta hebdomades abbreviatæ sunt super populum tuum]] (that is, weeks of lunar years), that [[Dan 9:24|iniquity may be abolished|deleatur iniquitas]], and [[Dan 9:24|vision and prophecy may be fulfilled|impleatur visio et prophetia]], and the Saint of saints be anointed. The manner of this coming too, namely that Christ came and lived among men in the greatest poverty and humility, was described through Jeremias: [[Jer 14:8|why wilt thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man turning in to lodge?|Quare quasi colonus venturus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum?]] [*colonus*, a tiller of another's land]. And through Zacharias: [[Matt 21:5|Behold thy king cometh to thee, meek|Ecce Rex tuus veniet tibi mansuetus]]; [[Zach 9:9|he is poor|ipse pauper]] [Denis joins Zach 9:9 with the words of Matt 21:5]. And again the Psalmist: [[Ps 87:16|I am poor, and in labours from my youth|Pauper sum ego, et in laboribus a juventute mea]]. Further, of the place of His birth, through Micheas: [[Mich 5:2|And thou Bethlehem Ephrata|Et tu, Bethlehem Ephrata]], [[Mich 5:2|out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be the ruler in Israel|ex te mihi egredietur qui sit dominator in Israel]]. The manner of His conception too Isaias set forth: [[Is 7:14|Behold a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son|Ecce virgo concipiet et pariet filium]]; and again: [[Is 53:2|And he shall grow up as a tender plant before him, and as a root out of a thirsty ground|Ascendet, inquit, quasi virgultum coram eo, et quasi radix de terra sitienti]]. This is what the Psalmist prophesied: [[Ps 71:6|He shall come down like rain upon the fleece; and as showers falling gently upon the earth|Descendet sicut pluvia in vellus, et sicut stillicidia stillantia super terram]]. And of the passion and its time Daniel said: [[Dan 9:26|after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be slain|Post hebdomades sexaginta duas occidetur Christus]]; and Isaias: [[Is 53:5|he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our sins|Ipse vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra]], [[Is 53:7|he shall be led as a sheep to the slaughter|sicut ovis ad occisionem ducetur]]. And to sum up, there is hardly anything contained in the Gospel that is not found foretold in the Old Testament. For which reason the Apostle says that he was [[Rom 1:1|separated unto the gospel of God|segregatum in Evangelium]], [[Rom 1:2|Which he had promised before, by his prophets, in the holy scriptures|quod ante promiserat Deus per Prophetas suos in Scripturis sanctis]], concerning His Son[[Rom 1:3||]].

paras.t: Et non vultis venire ad me per fidem et obedientiam: secundum quod Psalmista hortatur, Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini. Propriæ ergo voluntatis obstinatio, est causa perfidiæ Judæorum. Ut vitam spiritualem habeatis, in præsenti per gratiam, et in futuro per gloriam.
paras.en: [[5:40|And you will not come to me|Et non vultis venire ad me]] by faith and obedience, as the Psalmist exhorts: [[Ps 33:6|Come ye to him and be enlightened|Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini]]. The obstinacy of their own will, then, is the cause of the Jews' faithlessness. [[5:40|that you may have life|Ut vitam spiritualem habeatis]], spiritual life, in the present by grace and in the future by glory.

paras.t: Et quia Christus jam multa de propria excellentia retulit, ne Judæi eum de jactantia increparent, subintulit: Claritatem ab hominibus non accipio, id est, humanam gloriam et laudem non requiro. Sed nonne Christus præcipit sibi a nobis serviri? Nonne jubet se adorari omnibusque præferri? Quomodo ergo non quærit claritatem ab homine? Et respondendum, quia secundum quod homo, non quæsivit nec quærit ista propter se, vel ex privato amore; sed ut Deus, exigit ista, tanquam Creator et princeps altissimus. Imo, ut homo, vult honorari, non ex vanitate, sed zelo justitiæ, secundum ordinationem voluntatis divinæ: sicut etiam justus prælatus, quamvis humilis, vult zelo justitiæ propter honorem Dei, cujus vices gerit, ut debita sibi a subditis reverentia impendatur. Omnis autem rationalis creatura bene disposita, finaliter quærit honorare Deum per laudem et obedientiam, ex sincero amore, et honorari a Deo per unionem cum ipso et collocationem in suo cælesti palatio. — Si ergo Christus, qui habet in vestimento et in femore suo scriptum, Rex regum et Dominus dominantium, non accepit ab hominibus claritatem: cur nos miseri, vitiis tabidi, ad omne malum proclives, vanitate seducimur, quærentes sciri, reputari, honorari, præesse? Odibilis coram Deo et hominibus est ista superbia. Hinc ad Hebræos ait Apostolus: Christus proposito sibi gaudio, sustinuit crucem, confusione contempta.
paras.en: And since Christ has now said many things of His own excellence, lest the Jews should rebuke Him for boasting He added: [[5:41|I receive not glory from men|Claritatem ab hominibus non accipio]], that is, I do not seek human glory and praise. But does not Christ command that He be served by us? Does He not bid that He be adored and set before all? How then does He not seek glory from man? The answer is that as man He did not and does not seek these things for His own sake or from private love; but as God He requires them, as Creator and most high Prince. Indeed as man He wills to be honoured, not from vanity but from zeal for justice, according to the ordering of the divine will: as a just prelate too, however humble, wills from zeal for justice, for the honour of God whose place he holds, that due reverence be paid him by his subjects. And every rational creature that is well disposed seeks in the end to honour God by praise and obedience from sincere love, and to be honoured by God through union with Him and a place in His heavenly palace. — If, then, Christ, who [[Apoc 19:16|hath on his garment and on his thigh written: KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS|habet in vestimento et in femore suo scriptum, Rex regum et Dominus dominantium]], did not receive glory from men, why are we wretches, wasting with vices and prone to every evil, led astray by vanity, seeking to be known, esteemed, honoured and set over others? [[Ecclus 10:7|Pride is hateful before God and men|Odibilis coram Deo et hominibus est ista superbia]]. Hence the Apostle says to the Hebrews that Christ, [[Heb 12:2|having joy set before him, endured the cross, despising the shame|proposito sibi gaudio, sustinuit crucem, confusione contempta]].

paras.t: Sed cognovi vos cognitione reprobationis, quia dilectionem Dei gratuitam ac meritoriam, quæ est virtus theologica et infusa: de qua dicit Apostolus, Finis præcepti est caritas de corde puro, et conscientia bona, et fide non ficta; non habetis in vobis, videlicet appetitu intellectivo seu voluntate, quæ est caritatis subjectum. Nihilo minus naturalem Dei dilectionem impii aliqui habent; non tamen damnati. Sine dilectione autem Dei gratuita, nihil est meritorium, prout Paulus testatur: Si linguis angelorum loquar et hominum, caritatem autem non habeam, nihil sum. Caritas est enim propria vita animæ, sicut in prima sua Canonica docet Joannes: Qui non diligit, manet in morte.
paras.en: [[5:42|But I know you|Sed cognovi vos]], with the knowledge of reprobation, [[5:42|that you have not the love of God|quia dilectionem Dei non habetis]], the freely given and meritorious love, which is a theological and infused virtue, of which the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 1:5|the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith|Finis præcepti est caritas de corde puro, et conscientia bona, et fide non ficta]]; [[5:42|in you|in vobis]], that is, in the intellective appetite or will, which is the subject of charity. None the less some of the wicked have a natural love of God, though the damned do not. But without the freely given love of God nothing is meritorious, as Paul testifies: [[1 Cor 13:1|If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity|Si linguis angelorum loquar et hominum, caritatem autem non habeam]], [[1 Cor 13:2|I am nothing|nihil sum]]. For charity is the soul's own life, as John teaches in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 3:14|He that loveth not abideth in death|Qui non diligit, manet in morte]].

paras.t: Ego veni in nomine Patris mei, id est in Patre meo, hoc est secundum voluntatem et ordinationem Patris æterni, ad honorem ipsius, cujus in omnibus dictis meis atque operibus beneplacitum impleo gloriamque requiro; et non accepistis me per fidem, dilectionem et obedientiam. Si alius venerit, id est, quia et quum Antichristus venerit, in nomine suo, hoc est, proprium honorem et gloriam quærens, non missus a Deo, sed se ipsum inæstimabili mentis tumore extollens supra omne quod dicitur Deus aut quod colitur, illum accipietis, credendo quod ipse sit Messias in lege promissus. In hunc enim errorem cadere meruistis, verum Filium Dei spernendo. Itaque quod ait, Si alius venerit, non dicitur dubitative; et quod addit, Illum accipietis, non dicitur ad Judæos quos Christus tunc præsentialiter loquebatur, qui jam diu occubuerunt, nisi sub persona illorum intelligendo communiter genus Judaici populi, quod primo et maxime adhærebit Antichristo, donec per Enoch et Eliam convertantur, et Antichristi falsitas detegatur.
paras.en: [[5:43|I am come in the name of my Father|Ego veni in nomine Patris mei]], that is, in My Father, according to the will and ordering of the eternal Father, for His honour, whose good pleasure I fulfil and whose glory I seek in all My words and works; [[5:43|and you receive me not|et non accepistis me]] by faith, love and obedience. [[5:43|if another shall come|Si alius venerit]], that is, since and when Antichrist shall come, [[5:43|in his own name|in nomine suo]], that is, seeking his own honour and glory, not sent by God, but with a swelling of mind beyond reckoning [[2 Thess 2:4|is lifted up above all that is called God or that is worshipped|extollens supra omne quod dicitur Deus aut quod colitur]], [[5:43|him you will receive|illum accipietis]], believing that he is the Messias promised in the law. For you have deserved to fall into this error by spurning the true Son of God. So when He says, *if another shall come*, it is not said in doubt; and when He adds, *him you will receive*, it is not said to the Jews to whom Christ was then speaking in person, who died long ago, except as understanding in their person the Jewish people in general, which will be the first and the most to cleave to Antichrist, until they are converted by Enoch and Elias and the falsehood of Antichrist is laid bare.

paras.t: Quomodo potestis vos credere fide formata, viva et operatoria, qui gloriam ab invicem accipitis cum affectu, et humanum favorem, terrenum honorem, propriam laudem optatis, quæritis et acceptatis, et gloriam quæ a solo Deo est, id est veram atque æternam felicitatem, non quæritis, virtuose vivendo? Constituistis enim vobis finem in rebus caducis et vanis, non in Deo benedicto. Videmus enim multos ambitiosos et arrogantes, fidem habere, et contra infideles armari: non ergo loquitur Christus de fide informi et vacua, sed formata.
paras.en: [[5:44|How can you believe|Quomodo potestis vos credere]] with formed faith, living and working, [[5:44|who receive glory one from another|qui gloriam ab invicem accipitis]] with affection, and desire, seek and accept human favour, earthly honour and your own praise, [[5:44|and the glory which is from God alone, you do not seek?|et gloriam quæ a solo Deo est, non quæritis?]], that is, true and eternal happiness, by living virtuously. For you have set your end in perishable and vain things, not in the blessed God. For we see many ambitious and arrogant men who have faith and take up arms against unbelievers: so Christ is not speaking of unformed and empty faith, but of formed faith.

paras.t: Elucescit autem ex his, quod vana gloria omne spirituale bonum impediat, et pestiferum valdeque grave crimen consistat. Propter quod dicit Psalmista: Quoniam Deus dissipavit ossa eorum qui hominibus placent, id est, placere desiderant; confusi sunt, quoniam Deus sprevit eos. Et Apostolus: Si hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem. Omnis ambitiosus et animosus similis est viro stulto qui ædificat domum suam supra arenam. Specialiter autem ambitiositas ista impedit Judæos a fide Christi. Quoniam enim scripturas Prophetarum solum litteraliter intelligunt, putant quod Christus in primo suo adventu, omnia regna mundi eis subjiciet: sicque temporalem principatum, terrenum honorem, humanam exaltationem sperant et cupiunt. Unde in Jesum paupertatis et humilitatis magistrum, omniumque temporalium contemptorem, credere noluerunt et nolunt. Itaque soli Deo placere, et ei dumtaxat displicere formidemus, et in solo Deo sit gloriatio nostra.
paras.en: From this it shines out that vainglory hinders every spiritual good and is a pestilent and very grave crime. For which reason the Psalmist says: [[Ps 52:6|For God hath scattered the bones of them that please men: they have been confounded, because God hath despised them|Quoniam Deus dissipavit ossa eorum qui hominibus placent, id est, placere desiderant; confusi sunt, quoniam Deus sprevit eos]] (*that please men*, that is, desire to please them). And the Apostle: [[Gal 1:10|If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ|Si hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem]]. Every ambitious and spirited man is [[Matt 7:26|like a foolish man that built his house upon the sand|similis est viro stulto qui ædificat domum suam supra arenam]]. And in particular this ambition keeps the Jews from faith in Christ. For since they understand the writings of the Prophets only according to the letter, they think that Christ at His first coming will make all the kingdoms of the world subject to them; and so they hope for and desire temporal rule, earthly honour and human exaltation. Hence they would not, and will not, believe in Jesus, the teacher of poverty and humility and the despiser of all temporal things. Let us, then, fear to please God alone, and to displease Him alone, and let our glorying be in God alone.

paras.t: Nolite putare quia ego accusaturus sim vos apud Patrem. Hoc ait Salvator, non quod ipse nequaquam accusabit Judæos, quum ipse sit judex et testis, qui alibi loquitur: Qui me erubuerit, hunc Filius hominis erubescet coram Patre et angelis. Unde per Jeremiam ait: Attende, Domine, et audi vocem adversariorum meorum. Numquid redditur pro bono malum, quia foderunt foveam animæ meæ? Nonne Christus accusavit Judæos, quum dixit passione instante, Nunc autem excusationem non habent de peccato suo, et oderunt me et Patrem meum gratis? Per hoc quippe Christus eos accusat, quod propriis verbis et actibus, imo et vulnerum suorum cicatricibus, quas servavit in testimonium contra ingratos, ostendit eos damnatione dignissimos. Sed idcirco dicit quod non accusabit eos, quia non ipse solus hoc faciet. Propter quod subditur: Est qui accusat vos, id est, damnatione dignos affirmat in suis scripturis, Moyses in quo vos speratis, hoc est, per cujus legem salvari confiditis sine meritis Christi. Putant enim Judæi observationem legis sufficere ad salutem. Multa autem sunt verba in libris Moysis, quibus probantur Judæi damnationem mereri.
paras.en: [[5:45|Think not that I will accuse you to the Father|Nolite putare quia ego accusaturus sim vos apud Patrem]]. The Saviour says this not because He will in no way accuse the Jews, since He is judge and witness, and says elsewhere: [[Luke 9:26|he that shall be ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of man shall be ashamed|Qui me erubuerit, hunc Filius hominis erubescet]] before the Father and the angels. Hence He says through Jeremias: [[Jer 18:19|Give heed to me, O Lord, and hear the voice of my adversaries|Attende, Domine, et audi vocem adversariorum meorum]]. [[Jer 18:20|Shall evil be rendered for good, because they have digged a pit for my soul?|Numquid redditur pro bono malum, quia foderunt foveam animæ meæ?]] Did not Christ accuse the Jews when, with the Passion at hand, He said: [[John 15:22|but now they have no excuse for their sin|Nunc autem excusationem non habent de peccato suo]], and [[John 15:24|hated both me and my Father|oderunt me et Patrem meum]] without cause? For in this Christ accuses them: that by His own words and acts, and indeed by the scars of His wounds, which He kept as a witness against the ungrateful, He shows them most worthy of damnation. But He says that He will not accuse them because He will not do it alone. For which reason it is added: [[5:45|There is one that accuseth you|Est qui accusat vos]], that is, declares you worthy of damnation in his writings, [[5:45|Moses, in whom you trust|Moyses in quo vos speratis]], that is, by whose law you trust to be saved without the merits of Christ. For the Jews think that keeping the law is enough for salvation. And there are many words in the books of Moses by which the Jews are proved to deserve damnation.

paras.t: Quod vero Moyses accusaturus est eos, Christus subjunxit. Si enim crederetis Moysi, crederetis forsitan et mihi. Si interrogaremus Judæos, an credant Moysi, constantissime responderent quod imo: et tamen Veritas hoc loco dicit contrarium. Simili modo, si interrogaremus hæreticos, an credant Christo, firmissime dicerent, Credimus: et tamen ita non est. Numquid Arius, Eunomius, Photinus, Sabellius, et similes eis, veram in Deo trinitatem Personarum negantes, crediderunt sermonibus Christi? Et tamen Judæi atque hæretici putant se credere istis. Sed dicendum breviter, quod Judæi credunt Moysi, secundum eum intellectum quo verba ejus exponunt. Et quoniam verba ejus male intelligunt, ideo non credunt ei secundum veritatem, sed secundum ipsorum deceptoriam opinionem: quemadmodum aliquis putat se videre colorem rubeum, quum videt album per nigrum. Quod vero Christus ait, Forsitan, non dicit dubitando, sed humanam libertatem insinuando, et sobrium modum loquendi docendo.
paras.en: That Moses will accuse them Christ added: [[5:46|For if you did believe Moses, you would perhaps believe me also|Si enim crederetis Moysi, crederetis forsitan et mihi]]. If we asked the Jews whether they believe Moses, they would answer most steadfastly that they do: and yet the Truth in this place says the contrary. In the same way, if we asked heretics whether they believe Christ, they would say most firmly, We believe: and yet it is not so. Did Arius, Eunomius, Photinus, Sabellius and the like, who denied the true trinity of Persons in God, believe the words of Christ? And yet Jews and heretics think that they believe them. But it must be said briefly that the Jews believe Moses according to the understanding with which they expound his words. And since they understand his words badly, they do not believe him according to the truth, but according to their own deceiving opinion: as someone thinks he sees red when he sees white through black. And when Christ says *perhaps*, He does not say it in doubt, but to hint at human freedom and to teach a sober way of speaking.

paras.t: De me enim ille scripsit. Multa namque scripsit Moyses de Christo, quædam verba aliorum narrando, quædam in propria persona prophetando, quædam figuraliter et occulte de mysteriis Christi et passione ejus, per sacramenta et cærimonialia legis insinuando. Primo modo scripsit de Christo in Genesi, quum recitat Deum dixisse ad Abraham, In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes; et quando Jacob dixit, Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda, etc.; itemque, Salutare tuum exspectabo, Domine; et in libro Numerorum, recitando vaticinia Balaam. Secundo modo scripsit de Christo in Deuteronomio: Prophetam suscitabit vobis Dominus, etc. Accusat quoque Judæos, adjungens: Omnis qui non audierit Prophetam illum, peribit de populo suo. Tertio modo scripsit de Christo in Exodo atque Levitico, loquens de ritu agni paschalis et ceteris sacrificiis: per quæ passio Christi præfigurabatur.
paras.en: [[5:46|for he wrote of me|De me enim ille scripsit]]. For Moses wrote many things of Christ: some by relating the words of others, some by prophesying in his own person, and some by hinting figuratively and in a hidden way at the mysteries of Christ and His passion through the sacraments and ceremonies of the law. In the first way he wrote of Christ in Genesis, when he relates that God said to Abraham, [[Gen 22:18|in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes]]; and when Jacob said, [[Gen 49:10|The sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda|Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda]], etc.; and again, [[Gen 49:18|I will look for thy salvation, O Lord|Salutare tuum exspectabo, Domine]]; and in the book of Numbers, by relating the prophecies of Balaam[[Num 24:17||]]. In the second way he wrote of Christ in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 18:15|The Lord thy God will raise up to thee a PROPHET|Prophetam suscitabit vobis Dominus]], etc. And he accuses the Jews too, adding: [[Acts 3:23|every soul which will not hear that prophet shall be destroyed from among the people|Omnis qui non audierit Prophetam illum, peribit de populo suo]][[Deut 18:19||]] [Denis gives the words as St Peter cites them]. In the third way he wrote of Christ in Exodus and Leviticus, speaking of the rite of the paschal lamb and the other sacrifices[[Ex 12:3||]][[Lev 1:2||]], by which the passion of Christ was prefigured.

paras.t: Si autem illius litteris, id est scripturis, non creditis, quia nec intelligitis eas veraciter, quomodo verbis meis credetis? Et hoc rursus, sicut et cetera Christi eloquia, indiget sano intellectu, quia sic sonat quasi scripta seu testimonia Moysis essent magis credibilia atque authentica quam verba Christi. Est igitur sensus: Si illius litteris non creditis, quem æstimatis majoris auctoritatis esse quam me, et ad quem majorem affectum habetis, quomodo verbis meis credetis? quasi dicat: Quia illi non creditis, mihi credere non potestis. Potest etiam absolute intelligi, ut dicat verba Moysis credibiliora quam sua, quoniam erant minus incomprehensibilia, difficilia et supernaturalia, quam verba Christi, quæ omnem penitus rationem transcendunt.
paras.en: [[5:47|But if you do not believe his writings|Si autem illius litteris non creditis]], because you do not understand them truly, [[5:47|how will you believe my words?|quomodo verbis meis credetis?]] And this again, like Christ's other sayings, needs a sound understanding, since it sounds as though the writings or testimonies of Moses were more believable and authoritative than the words of Christ. The sense, then, is: If you do not believe the writings of him whom you think of greater authority than Me, and towards whom you have greater affection, how will you believe My words? As if He said: Because you do not believe him, you cannot believe Me. It can also be understood absolutely, as saying that the words of Moses were more believable than His own, since they were less incomprehensible, difficult and supernatural than the words of Christ, which wholly transcend all reason.

6.title: Expositio capituli sexti: Post hæc abiit Jesus trans mare Galilææ.
6.title_en: Exposition of the sixth chapter: “After these things Jesus went over the sea of Galilee.”

paras.t: Post hæc narrat Evangelista grande miraculum, quo omnipotentia Christi magnifice noscitur demonstrata, ejusque supernaturalis doctrina efficaciter roborata, ut supernaturalis assertio supernaturali firmaretur argumento.
paras.en: After this the Evangelist tells of a great miracle, by which the almighty power of Christ is known to have been splendidly shown, and his supernatural teaching strongly confirmed, so that a supernatural assertion might be made firm by a supernatural proof.

paras.t: Post hæc quas in præcedenti capitulo dicta gestaque feruntur, abiit Jesus a Jerusalem et Judæa. Abiit autem et navigavit trans mare Galilææ, quod est mare Tiberiadis, id est, mare istud, quod dicitur mare Galilææ, a provincia in qua situm est, dicitur etiam mare Tiberiadis, ab urbe nomine Tiberias, quæ sita est in littore hujus maris. Abiit autem Jesus diversis ex causis. Primo, secundum quod hic insinuatur, cedens persecutioni Judæorum, ne ante tempus præfixum ab eis occideretur. Secundo, cedens furori Herodis. Ut enim in Matthæo legitur, Jesus audita decollatione Joannis, fecit quæ jam refert Evangelista. Tertio, ut discipuli sui post laborem paululum repausarent: quia ut scribitur in Marco, Erant qui ibant et redibant, et nec spatium manducandi habebant. Unde Christus ait discipulis: Venite seorsum in desertum locum, et requiescite pusillum.
paras.en: [[6:1|After these things|Post hæc]] which are related as said and done in the preceding chapter, [[6:1|Jesus went|abiit Jesus]] from Jerusalem and Judea. He went, and sailed [[6:1|over the sea of Galilee, which is that of Tiberias|trans mare Galilææ, quod est mare Tiberiadis]], that is, this sea, which is called the sea of Galilee from the province in which it lies, is also called the sea of Tiberias from a city named Tiberias, which lies on the shore of this sea. Jesus went away for divers reasons. First, as is suggested here, yielding to the persecution of the Jews, lest he be killed by them before the appointed time. Second, yielding to the fury of Herod: for, as is read in Matthew, Jesus, on hearing of the beheading of John, did what the Evangelist now relates[[Matt 14:13||]]. Third, that his disciples might rest a little after their labour: for, as is written in Mark, [[Mark 6:31|For there were many coming and going: and they had not so much as time to eat|Erant qui ibant et redibant, et nec spatium manducandi habebant]]. Hence Christ says to the disciples: [[Mark 6:31|Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little|Venite seorsum in desertum locum, et requiescite pusillum]].

paras.t: Et sequebatur eum multitudo magna, quia videbant signa, hoc est miraculosas curationes, quæ faciebat super his, id est in eis hominibus, qui infirmabantur. Hæc fuit una ratio ob quam sequebantur eum. Diversi tamen diversis de causis Christum corporaliter sequebantur: quidam, ut aliquid reprehensionis in verbis aut actibus ejus invenirent, quemadmodum Pharisæi et Scribæ invidiosi; quidam, ut instruerentur et vitam suam corrigerent, ut studiosi ac pœnitentes; quidam, ut signa viderent et nova audirent, ut curiosi; quidam, ut curarentur; quidam, ut suis sanitatem acquirerent, sicut de regulo dictum est; quidam, ut corporaliter reficerentur. Et quoniam Dominus Jesus etiam secundum corpus speciosus valde et eloquentissimus fuit, et optime habitudinis, verisimile est quod multi sequebantur eum delectati specie et eloquentia ejus. Denique, secundum Matthæum, prædicta multitudo de civitatibus secuta est Christum pedestris. Ex quo elicitur quod plebeii fuerunt pro majori parte. Et ut Marcus testatur, quum cognovissent quod Jesus esset, de omnibus civitatibus concurrerunt illuc, et. prævenerunt discipulos Christi. In quo patet fervens eorum ad Christum affectio, ac prompta devotio, saltem quorumdam.
paras.en: [[6:2|And a great multitude followed him, because they saw the miracles|Et sequebatur eum multitudo magna, quia videbant signa]], that is, miraculous cures, [[6:2|which he did on them that were diseased|quæ faciebat super his qui infirmabantur]], that is, on those men who were sick. This was one reason for which they followed him. But divers men followed Christ in the body for divers causes: some, to find something to blame in his words or deeds, like the envious Pharisees and Scribes[[Matt 22:15||]][[Luke 11:53||]]; some, to be instructed and to amend their life, like the earnest and the penitent[[Matt 19:16||]]; some, to see signs and hear new things, like the curious[[Matt 12:38||]][[Matt 16:1||]]; some, to be cured; some, to obtain health for their own, as was said of the ruler[[John 4:46||]]; some, to be fed in the body. And since the Lord Jesus was also very beautiful in body and most eloquent, and of the best bearing, it is likely that many followed him delighted by his beauty and his eloquence. Further, according to Matthew, the multitude spoken of followed Christ on foot out of the cities[[Matt 14:13||]]: from which it is gathered that they were for the most part common people. And as Mark testifies, [[Mark 6:33|many knew: and they ran flocking thither foot from all the cities, and were there before them|cognovissent quod Jesus esset, de omnibus civitatibus concurrerunt illuc, et. prævenerunt]] [Denis: “when they knew that it was Jesus, they ran together there from all the cities, and were before Christ's disciples”]. In this is plain their fervent affection towards Christ and their ready devotion, at least of some of them.

paras.t: Subiit ergo in montem Jesus, ut locus corresponderet locato. Christus enim propter sanctissimæ vitæ excellentiam, propter miraculorum eminentiam, propter contemplationis celsitudinem, propter caritatis omniumque virtutum incomparabilem sublimitatem, mons appellatur. De quo per Danielem asseritur, quod lapis abscissus sine manibus, crevit in montem magnum, implevitque universam superficiem terræ. Mons ergo ascendit in montem, implens ad litteram illud quod dicitur per Isaiam: Super montem excelsum ascende tu, qui evangelizas Sion. Ascendit ergo in montem, qui est locus orationi, contemplationi instructionique aptus, ut et nos similiter faciamus tempore opportuno. Opportunitas equidem loci plurimum confert ad devotionem. Ascendit quoque in montem, docens nos suo exemplo terrena ista atque carnalia abjeetare, et cœlestia ac divina toto affectu requirere: quatenus cum Apostolo quæ sursum sunt quæramus ac sapiamus, non qua super terram; et qua retro sunt obliti, in anteriora extendamus nos ipsos, omnia sensibilia vana atque caduca arbitrantes ut stercora, ut super invisibili Deo ardenti de siderio uniamur. Et ibi sedebat cum discipulis suis, docens eos, et latitudinem terræ quam condidit circeumspiciens, magis autem habitatoribus terræ compatiens, eisque auxiliari proponens.
paras.en: [[6:3|Jesus therefore went up into a mountain|Subiit ergo in montem Jesus]], so that the place might answer to the one placed in it. For Christ, because of the excellence of his most holy life, the eminence of his miracles, the height of his contemplation, and the incomparable sublimity of his charity and of all virtues, is called a mountain. Of whom it is said by Daniel that a stone cut out without hands grew into a great mountain and filled the whole face of the earth[[Dan 2:35||]]. The mountain, then, goes up into the mountain, fulfilling to the letter what is said by Isaias: [[Is 40:9|Get thee up upon a high mountain, thou that bringest good tidings to Sion|Super montem excelsum ascende tu, qui evangelizas Sion]]. He went up, then, into a mountain, which is a place fit for prayer, contemplation and teaching, that we too may do likewise at a fitting time: for the fitness of the place helps devotion very much. He went up into a mountain also teaching us by his example to cast away these earthly and carnal things, and to seek heavenly and divine things with all our affection, so that with the Apostle we may seek and [[Col 3:2|Mind the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth|sapiamus, non quæ super terram]] [Denis: “seek and mind the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth”], and, [[Phil 3:13|Forgetting the things that are behind and stretching forth myself to those that are before|quæ retro sunt obliti, in anteriora extendamus nos ipsos]], [[Phil 3:8|count them but as dung|arbitrantes ut stercora]] all things of sense, vain and perishing, so that we may be united with ardent desire to the invisible God above. [[6:3|and there he sat with his disciples|Et ibi sedebat cum discipulis suis]], teaching them, and looking round on the breadth of the earth which he had made, but still more, having compassion on the inhabitants of the earth and purposing to help them.

paras.t: Erat autem proximum Pascha, dies festus Judæorum, id est, de propinquo jam imminebat. Porro, ut Beda ait, inter decollationem Joannis et Christi passionem, unius anni exstitit spatium. Et sic istud fuit Pascha secundum, circa quod decollatus est Joannes: in quo Christus non fuit in Jerusalem, cedens adversariis suis. Nam, sicut sepe observavit legalia, ostendendo se hominem verum factum sub lege; sic interdum prætermisit ea, ostendens se verum Deum ac legislatorem supra legem. Quia hic dicitur, Erat proximum Pascha, evangelium istud legitur in medio Quadragesima, propinquante paschali solennitate.
paras.en: [[6:4|Now the pasch, the festival day of the Jews, was near at hand|Erat autem proximum Pascha, dies festus Judæorum]], that is, was now close at hand. Further, as Bede says, between the beheading of John and the passion of Christ there was the space of one year. And so this was the second Pasch, about which John was beheaded: at which Christ was not in Jerusalem, giving way to his adversaries[[Matt 14:13||]]. For, as he often kept the ordinances of the law, showing himself to be true man, [[Gal 4:4|made under the law|factum sub lege]], so at times he passed them over, showing himself to be true God and lawgiver above the law. Because it is said here, *the pasch was near*, this gospel is read in the middle of Lent, as the paschal solemnity draws near.

paras.t: Quum sublevasset ergo oculos Jesus, qui oculis vagus non fuit, sed summe compositus; nee sine ingenti causa circumspexit, sed in omnibus universæ maturitatis et probitatis dedit exemplum; et vidisset quia multitudo maxima, videlicet quinque millia virorum, præter mulieres et pueros, venit ad eum, dixit ad Philippum, qui primo omnium dicitur a Christo ad apostolatum vocatus. Unde nunc forte propter familiaritatem et caritatis ostensionem, specialiter dirigit sermonem ad eum. Aliqui tamen affirmant quod Philippus ceteris discipulis rudior fuit, ideo magis indiguit informari: et hinc Christus eum interrogat, non quasi ignorans, sed informare intendens. Unde ememus panes ut manducent hi ? Noverat Christus non adesse pecuniam ad emendum tot panes sufficientem, quoniam pau per fuit, et parum vel nihil secum detulit de argento et auro.
paras.en: [[6:5|When Jesus therefore had lifted up his eyes|Quum sublevasset ergo oculos Jesus]], who was not wandering with his eyes, but supremely composed, and did not look about without great cause, but in all things gave an example of every maturity and uprightness; [[6:5|and seen that a very great multitude cometh to him|et vidisset quia multitudo maxima venit ad eum]], namely five thousand men, besides women and children, [[6:5|he said to Philip|dixit ad Philippum]], who is said to have been called by Christ to the apostolate first of all[[John 1:43||]]. Hence now, perhaps for familiarity and to show his charity, he directs his words especially to him. Some, however, affirm that Philip was more untaught than the other disciples, and so had more need of being informed: and that this is why Christ questions him, not as one who did not know, but meaning to inform. [[6:5|Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat|Unde ememus panes ut manducent hi]]? Christ knew that there was not money enough at hand to buy so much bread, since he was poor, and carried little or no silver and gold with him.

paras.t: Hoc autem dicebat tentans eum, tentatione pie probationis ordinata ad instructionem, qua tentavit et Abraham: non tentatione seduetionis ordinate ad confusionem, de qua Jacobus ait in sua Canonica: Nemo quum tentatur, dicat quia a Deo tentatur; Deus enim intentator malorum est. De prima tentatione scriptum est in libro Sapientiæ: Deus tentavit justos, et invenit illos dignos se; in Deuteronomio quoque dicitur, Recordaberis cuncti itineris per quod adduxit te Dominus Deus tuus, ut affligeret te atque tentaret. De secunda oramus: Et ne nos inducas in tentationem. — Sed quum tentare sit experimentum de tentato accipere, quomodo Deus aliquem tentat, qui de nullo accipit experimentum, quippe quum ei omnia antequam fiant, patescant? Et respondendum, quod etiam in Scripturis dicitur Deus experiri, seu aliqua facere ad experiendum, juxta illud Judicum: Dimisit Dominus Chananæos, ut in ipsis experiretur Israelem, utrum custodiret mandata Domini, an non. Dicitur itaque Deus sumere experimentum, non ut ei aliquid innotescat, sed ut tentatus agnoscat se ipsum, vet alii ad ejus notitiam perducantur. Sic ergo tentavit Philippum, ejus ignorantiam demonstrando, non solum ad instructionem Philippi, sed omnium discipulorum, quatenus miraculum magis ostenderetur, et virtus Christi agnosceretur. Perfectos autem tentat Deus, ut eorum perfectio aliis pateat ad exemplum, ut Job et Tobiam; imperfectos vero, ut eorum imperfectio eis elareat ad propriam humiliationem. — Ipse enim sciebat quid esset facturus: ideo non sciscitabatur consilium vel auxilium postulando.
paras.en: [[6:6|And this he said to try him|Hoc autem dicebat tentans eum]], with the temptation of loving proof, ordered to instruction, with which he tempted Abraham too[[Gen 22:1||]]: not with the temptation of seduction, ordered to confusion, of which James says in his Canonical Epistle: [[Jas 1:13|Let no man, when he is tempted, say that he is tempted by God. For God is not a tempter of evils|Nemo quum tentatur, dicat quia a Deo tentatur; Deus enim intentator malorum est]]. Of the first temptation it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 3:5|God hath tried them, and found them worthy of himself|Deus tentavit justos, et invenit illos dignos se]] [Denis: “God hath tried the just, and found them worthy of himself”]; in Deuteronomy also it is said: [[Deut 8:2|And thou shalt remember all the way through which the Lord thy God hath brought thee for forty years through the desert, to afflict thee and to prove thee|Recordaberis cuncti itineris per quod adduxit te Dominus Deus tuus, ut affligeret te atque tentaret]] [Denis omits “for forty years through the desert”] [the margin prints Deut. vii, 2; the words are those of Deut 8:2]. Of the second we pray: [[Matt 6:13|And lead us not into temptation|Et ne nos inducas in tentationem]]. But since to tempt is to take proof of the one tempted, how does God tempt anyone, who takes proof of no one, since all things lie open to him before they come to be? The answer is that in the Scriptures too God is said to make trial, or to do some things in order to make trial, according to that of Judges: [[Judg 3:4|And he left them, that he might try Israel by them, whether they would hear the commandments of the Lord, which he had commanded their fathers, by the hand of Moses, or not|Dimisit Dominus Chananæos, ut in ipsis experiretur Israelem, utrum custodiret mandata Domini, an non]] [Denis: “The Lord left the Chanaanites, that by them he might try Israel, whether he would keep the commandments of the Lord, or not”]. God, then, is said to take proof, not that anything may become known to him, but that the one tempted may know himself, or that others may be brought to know him. So, then, he tempted Philip by showing his ignorance, not only for the instruction of Philip but of all the disciples, so that the miracle might be the more shown and the power of Christ acknowledged. God tempts the perfect so that their perfection may lie open to others for an example, as Job and Tobias[[Tob 2:12||]]; but the imperfect, so that their imperfection may be clear to them for their own humbling. [[6:6|for he himself knew what he would do|Ipse enim sciebat quid esset facturus]]: so he was not inquiring by asking for counsel or help.

paras.t: Respondit ei Philippus: Ducentorum denariorum panes non sufficiunt eis, ut unusquisque modicum quid accipiat, id est, parvum frustum manducet. Tanquam diceret: Non habemus pretium ad emendum, nec possumus eis providere: ideirco remitte eos ad loca habitabilia, ut sibi ipsis provideant. Quanti valoris fuerint isti denarii, non exprimitur.
paras.en: [[6:7|Philip answered him: Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them that every one may take a little|Respondit ei Philippus: Ducentorum denariorum panes non sufficiunt eis, ut unusquisque modicum quid accipiat]], that is, may eat a small morsel. As though he said: We have not the price to buy, nor can we provide for them: therefore send them away to inhabited places, so that they may provide for themselves. How much these pence were worth is not stated.

paras.t: Dicit ei unus ex discipulis ejus, Andreas frater Simonis Petri. Ad laudem Andreæ hoc pertinet, quod principis Apostolorum exstitit frater. Unde et Judas in sua Canonica vocat se fratrem Jacobi, tanquam dignioris, non ad jactantiam, sed ut a fidelibus quibus scripsit diligentius audiretur. Est puer unus hic: qui puer vocatur, non tam propter ætatis parvitatem, quam propter puritatem et innocentiam: ad quam pueritiam obligamur, Christo dicente, Nisi conversi fueritis, et efficiamini sicut parvuli, non intrabitis in regnum cœlorum. Unde hortatur Apostolus: Nolite pueri effici sensibus, sed malitia parvuli estote. Denique in Scripturis dicitur aliquis puer tripliciter. Primo, propter stoliditatem et inconstantiam, Isaia teste: Puer centum annorum morietur, hoc est senex fatuus. Secundo. propter puritatem et innocentiam, ut ibi Laudate, pueri, Dominum. Tertio, propter ætatem permodieam, secundum quod Lucas ait: Puer Jesus crescebat. Qui habet quinque panes hordeaceos. Ecce quali cibo uti solebat Christus eum suis discipulis. Condemnata est ergo deliciositas, gulositas atque carnalitas nostra. Et duos pisces. Sed hæc quid sunt inter tantos: id est, parum vel nihil proderunt multitudini tantæ. Joannes, qui ultimo scripsit evangelium atque historiam istam, in aliquibus videtur ab aliis Evangelistis discordare. Sed illa facillime solvuntur, quia Joannes magis determinate et peculiariter recitat factum istud, quam alii; ideo dicit dictum ab uno discipulo, puta Philippo vel Andrea, quod alii Evangelistæ scribunt a discipulis communiter dictum. Tota enim societas fertur facere pati vel dicere, quod facit, sustinet, vel dicit pars ejus.
paras.en: [[6:8|One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, saith to him|Dicit ei unus ex discipulis ejus, Andreas frater Simonis Petri]]. It belongs to the praise of Andrew that he was the brother of the prince of the Apostles. Hence Jude too in his Canonical Epistle calls himself the brother of James[[Jude 1:1||]], as of one more worthy, not for boasting, but that he might be heard more carefully by the faithful to whom he wrote. [[6:9|There is a boy here|Est puer unus hic]]: who is called a boy not so much because of the smallness of his age as because of his purity and innocence: to which childhood we are bound, Christ saying, [[Matt 18:3|unless you be converted, and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven|Nisi conversi fueritis, et efficiamini sicut parvuli, non intrabitis in regnum cœlorum]]. Hence the Apostle exhorts: [[1 Cor 14:20|do not become children in sense. But in malice be children|Nolite pueri effici sensibus, sed malitia parvuli estote]]. Further, in the Scriptures one is called a boy in three ways. First, for dullness and inconstancy, as Isaias testifies: [[Is 65:20|the child shall die a hundred years old|Puer centum annorum morietur]], that is, a foolish old man. Second, for purity and innocence, as there: [[Ps 112:1|Praise the Lord, ye children|Laudate, pueri, Dominum]]. Third, for very small age, according to what Luke says: [[Luke 2:40|And the child grew|Puer Jesus crescebat]] [Denis: “The child Jesus grew”] [the margin is read as Luc. i, 80, of John the Baptist; the words fit Luke 2:40, of Jesus]. [[6:9|that hath five barley loaves|Qui habet quinque panes hordeaceos]]. See what food Christ was wont to use with his disciples: our daintiness, gluttony and carnality are therefore condemned. [[6:9|and two fishes. But what are these among so many|Et duos pisces. Sed hæc quid sunt inter tantos]]: that is, they will be of little or no use to so great a multitude. John, who wrote his gospel and this history last, seems in some things to disagree with the other Evangelists. But these are very easily solved: for John relates this deed more precisely and particularly than the others, and so says that something was said by one disciple, namely Philip or Andrew, which the other Evangelists write was said by the disciples in common[[Matt 14:17||]][[Mark 6:38||]][[Luke 9:13||]]. For the whole company is said to do, suffer or say what a part of it does, undergoes or says.

paras.t: Dixit ergo Jesus: Facite homines discumbere, id est ad manducandum ordinate sedere. Unde in Marco habetur, quod Y præcepit ut. facerent eos accumbere secundum contubernia sua. Erat autem fœnum multum in loco: et sic locus mollior et aptior fuit ad sedendum atque vescendum. Fuitque viride fœnum, secundum Marcum. Unde per fœnum intelligitur recens herba, seu gramen terra quale solet esse circa Pascha.
paras.en: [[6:10|Then Jesus said: Make the men sit down|Dixit ergo Jesus: Facite homines discumbere]], that is, sit down in order to eat. Hence in Mark it is had that [[Mark 6:39|he commanded them that they should make them all sit down by companies|præcepit ut. facerent eos accumbere secundum contubernia]] [Denis: “he commanded that they should make them sit down by their companies”]. [[6:10|Now, there was much grass in the place|Erat autem fœnum multum in loco]]: and so the place was softer and fitter for sitting and eating. And the grass was green, according to Mark[[Mark 6:39||]]: hence by *fœnum* [hay; the Douay-Rheims has “grass”] is understood fresh herbage, or grass of the ground such as there usually is about the Pasch.

paras.t: Discubuerunt ergo viri, per quinquagenos et centenos, ut dicitur in Marco, numero quasi quinque millia. Hoc dicit Joannes, quia fortassis erant paulo plures vel pauciores. Alii tamen Evangelistæ simpliciter asserunt quod erant quinque millia, non curantes de tali excessu, vel defectu tantillo. Consuetudo enim Scripturæ est, ut ponendo notabilem quantitatem in magnitudine vel multitudine, non curet de modico quod forte superfuit aut defuit. Sic enim in veteri Testamento dicuntur homines tot vel tot annis vixisse, et raro vel nunquam fit mentio nisi de annis, quum tamen non sit verisimile quod omnes illi vixerunt tot annis præcise, quasi eodem die morientes quo nati fuerunt. Preterea dicuntur viri, omnes masculini sexus, a viginti annis et supra, valentes ad bella procedere. De mulieribus vero et parvulis, qui forsitan numerum virorum vicerunt, non fit mentio, quia secundum consuetudinem legis, soli viri numerari consueverunt.
paras.en: [[6:10|The men therefore sat down|Discubuerunt ergo viri]], [[Mark 6:40|by hundreds and by fifties|per centenos et quinquagenos]] [Denis: “by fifties and hundreds”], as is said in Mark, [[6:10|in number about five thousand|numero quasi quinque millia]]. John says this because perhaps there were a few more or fewer. The other Evangelists, however, simply assert that there were five thousand[[Matt 14:21||]][[Mark 6:44||]], not caring about so slight an excess or defect. For it is the custom of Scripture, in giving a notable quantity in size or number, not to care about a little that may have been over or short. So in the Old Testament men are said to have lived so many or so many years, and rarely or never is mention made of anything but years, though it is not likely that all of them lived exactly so many years, as though dying on the same day on which they were born. Further, *men* means all of the male sex from twenty years old and upward, able to go forth to war[[Num 1:3||]]. Of the women and little ones, who perhaps outnumbered the men, no mention is made, because by the custom of the law only men were wont to be numbered[[Mark 6:44||]].

paras.t: Accepit ergo Jesus panes quinque in sanctas et venerabiles manus suas, organa unitæ Deitatis; et quum gratias egisset secundum quod homo, Deo Patri, vel summæ Trinitati, a qua omne bonum ex tempore sibi collatum accepit, distribuit discumbentibus, id est, per discipulos anteponi præcepit turbis illuc sedentibus, non jam dumtaxat quinque panes, sed et illud quod et ipse sua divina potestate, vel creando, vel multiplicando adjecit. Similiter et ex piscibus duobus, jam multiplicatis usque ad quantitatem quasi innumerabilium piscium, distribuit per manum discipulorum discumbentibus, quantum volebant, id est optabant, discumbentes, videlicet sufficienter, usque ad satietatem ipsorum.
paras.en: [[6:11|And Jesus took the loaves|Accepit ergo Jesus panes quinque]], the five, into his holy and venerable hands, the instruments of the united Godhead; [[6:11|and when he had given thanks|et quum gratias egisset]], as man, to God the Father, or to the supreme Trinity, from which he received every good conferred on him in time, [[6:11|he distributed to them that were set down|distribuit discumbentibus]], that is, he commanded that through the disciples there be set before the crowds sitting there, not now only five loaves, but also what he himself added by his divine power, either by creating or by multiplying. [[6:11|In like manner also of the fishes|Similiter et ex piscibus]], the two, now multiplied to the quantity of almost countless fishes, he distributed by the hand of the disciples to those sitting down, [[6:11|as much as they would|quantum volebant]], that is, wished, those sitting down, namely sufficiently, until they were satisfied.

paras.t: Ut autem impleti sunt, id est, discumbentibus copiose refectis ac saturatis, dixit discipulis suis: Colligite qua superaverunt fragmenta, id est, famem seu appetitum comedentium vicerunt, ita quod amplius manducare non poterant; vel, Qua superaverunt, id est, superfluxerunt edentibus; ne pereant, sed pauperibus remeantibus pro viatico conferantur. Unde Christus docuit hoc exemplo reliquias alimentorum prudenter servari, utiliterque expendi.
paras.en: [[6:12|And when they were filled|Ut autem impleti sunt]], that is, when those sitting down had been plentifully refreshed and satisfied, [[6:12|he said to his disciples: gather up the fragments that remain|dixit discipulis suis: Colligite quæ superaverunt fragmenta]], that is, which overcame the hunger or appetite of those eating, so that they could eat no more; or, *which remain*, that is, which were over for those eating; [[6:12|lest they be lost|ne pereant]], but be given to the poor going home, for provision on the way. So Christ taught by this example that the remains of food should be prudently kept and usefully spent.

paras.t: Collegerunt ergo, Apostoli præcipue, et impleverunt duodecim cophinos fragmentorum, videlicet quilibet Apostolus cophinum suum, si tamen soli Apostoli collegerunt: quod non apparet, quia propter multitudinem manducantium diu occupati fuissent in circumeundo et congregando. — Sed numquid increata Dei sapientia Christus, attingens a fine usque ad finem, et in numero, mensura ac pondere cuncta constituens, sine alto mysterio ordinavit ut duodecim cophini fragmentorum secundum duodenum numerum Apostolorum remanerent? Cur ergo sic contigit? Non plane a casu, sed eo moderante, quo operante facta est multiplicatio præmemorata. Palam est enim quod per panem designetur salutaris doctrina, ad cujus gustum invitat Sapientia dicens: Venite, comedite panem meum. Per fragmenta autem panum, signantur participationes imperfecte ipsius doctrinæ perfecte. Perfecta vero doctrina convenit Christo. Apostoli vero participando doctrinam Christi, quasi fragmenta et partes perfectæ doctrinæ a fonte sapientiæ collegerunt. Horum fragmentorum vasa seu cophini, erant corda Apostolorum, in quibus per totum mundum fragmenta sapientiæ Christi tulerunt, disperserunt et communicaverunt. Unde ad præfigurandum tantum mysterium, impleti sunt duodecim cophini fragmentorum, juxta numerum beatissimorum Apostolorum.
